payload.markdown: Slide 3 of your deck defines the vocabulary: a **leaf** has no children, a **subtree** is a node plus all its descendants, and the **height** of a tree is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. Slide 4 adds the core rule: for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are larger — distinct keys only. That rule is what makes searching possible: at each node you decide left or right, halving the possibilities. Inserting keys in sorted order (1, 2, 3, …) breaks this advantage: slide 8 warns that it builds a chain of height n − 1, turning every operation into O(n). You already know from heaps that a balanced shape matters; a BST that stays balanced keeps search, insert and delete at O(log n).

payload.intro: You'll work through search, insert and delete on the BST from slide 4: root 50, left child 30, right child 70, and leaves 20, 40, 60, 80. Keep the tree diagram open — each step changes the tree or tells you where to look.

steps.title: Search for key 60 iteratively
steps.detail_markdown: Start at the root (node with key 50). 60 > 50, so move to the right child (70). 60 < 70, so move to the left child (60). 60 === 60, stop. Return the node. The loop from slide 5: while (node !== null && key !== node.key) node = key < node.key ? node.left : node.right.
steps.warning: If you compare key !== node.key before checking null, a missing key causes a null reference error. The slide's loop checks null first.

steps.title: Search for key 55 (absent key)
steps.detail_markdown: Start at 50. 55 > 50 → go to 70. 55 < 70 → go to 60. 55 < 60 → go to 60's left child, which is null. The loop exits with node === null. Return null.
steps.warning: None — this is the normal absent-key case.

steps.title: Insert key 55 into the tree
steps.detail_markdown: Slide 5 says: search for the key, then attach a new leaf where the search fell off. Search for 55: 50 → 70 → 60 → null at 60's left. Create a new node with key 55 and set 60.left = that node.
steps.warning: If you insert a key that already exists, the search finds it and you must decide the policy — slide 4 assumes distinct keys, so duplicates are not inserted.
steps.check: Search for 55 now returns the new node, not null.

steps.title: Delete leaf 20
steps.detail_markdown: Slide 7: leaf case — just remove it. Find node 20 (50 → 30 → 20). 20 has no children. Set 30.left = null. The node is gone.
steps.warning: You must find the parent (30) to update its child pointer. If you only null the node variable, the tree is unchanged.

steps.title: Delete node 30 (one child — 40)
steps.detail_markdown: Find node 30. It has one child: 40. Slide 7 says replace the node by its child. Set the parent's (50's) left pointer to 30's child (40). Now 50.left = 40.
steps.warning: If the node is the root and has one child, the root pointer itself must change — not a parent's left or right.
steps.check: Search for 30 returns null; 40 is still reachable from the root.

steps.title: Delete root 50 (two children)
steps.detail_markdown: Slide 7: copy the in-order successor (smallest key in the right subtree) into the node, then delete the successor. The right subtree of 50 is rooted at 70; its smallest key is 60 (70 → 60). Copy 60 into the root (root.key = 60). Now delete the original 60 node, which has one child (80). Replace 70.left with 60's child (80). Tree root is now 60.
steps.warning: The successor might have a right child; you must handle that deletion with the one-child rule. Never copy the successor's children — only its key.
steps.check: Root key is 60; searching for 50 returns null; 80 is still present.

payload.title: BST operation checklist

items.text: Search loop checks null before key comparison
items.why: Prevents null reference error on absent key

items.text: Insert creates a new leaf node at the null child where search fell off
items.why: Ensures the BST property holds — the new node is placed correctly

items.text: Delete leaf: parent's child pointer set to null
items.why: Otherwise the parent still references the deleted node

items.text: Delete one-child: parent's pointer set to the node's only child
items.why: Splices the node out while keeping its subtree attached

items.text: Delete two-child: copy successor's key, then delete successor
items.why: Preserves BST property — successor is the smallest key larger than the node's

items.text: Successor deletion uses one-child or leaf rule
items.why: The successor has at most one child (right), so the two-child case never recurses

payload.instructions_markdown: Implement `search`, `insert`, and `deleteNode` for a BST. Use the iterative search loop from slide 5. For insert, search for the key and attach a new leaf where the search fell off — if the tree is empty, return a new node as the root. For delete, handle the three cases exactly as slide 7 describes: leaf (just remove), one child (replace by child), two children (copy in-order successor's key, then delete the successor). The tests build a tree and verify each operation.

tests.name: search finds inserted key
tests.call: (function() { var root = insert(null, 50); root = insert(root, 30); root = insert(root, 70); return search(root, 30).key; })()

tests.name: search returns null for absent key
tests.call: (function() { var root = insert(null, 50); root = insert(root, 30); return search(root, 40); })()

tests.name: delete leaf
tests.call: (function() { var root = insert(null, 50); root = insert(root, 30); root = insert(root, 70); root = deleteNode(root, 30); return search(root, 30); })()

tests.name: delete node with two children
tests.call: (function() { var root = insert(null, 50); root = insert(root, 30); root = insert(root, 70); root = insert(root, 20); root = insert(root, 40); root = insert(root, 60); root = insert(root, 80); root = deleteNode(root, 50); return root.key; })()

hints: For search: start at root, loop while node is not null and key doesn't match, go left or right.
For insert: if root is null, return new TreeNode(key). Otherwise walk down like search, but keep a parent pointer so you can attach the new node.
For delete two-child: find the in-order successor by going right once then left as far as possible. Copy its key into the current node, then delete the successor (which has at most one child).

assessments.prompt: Insert the keys 55, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35 in this order into an initially empty BST. Draw the final tree (describe it in text, e.g., 'root is 55, left child is 30, ...'). Then delete key 30 using the in-order successor and describe the resulting tree. Explain why the in-order successor method preserves the BST property.

answer_key.reference_answer: After insertions: root is 55. 55.left = 30, 55.right = 70. 30.left = 20, 30.right = 40. 70.left = 60, 70.right = 80. 40.left = 35. After deleting 30: the in-order successor of 30 is 35 (smallest key in 30's right subtree). Copy 35 into node 30. Delete the original 35 node (leaf). Result: root 55, 55.left = 35, 35.left = 20, 35.right = 40 (no left child), 40.left = null, 55.right = 70, 70.left = 60, 70.right = 80. The successor is the smallest key larger than 30, so all keys in the left subtree of 30 are smaller than 35, and all keys in the right subtree of 30 are larger than 35 — the BST property holds. The successor has at most one child, so its deletion is straightforward.

rubric.excellent: Describes a valid BST with root 55, left subtree containing 30 (with children 20 and 40, where 40 has left child 35), and right subtree containing 70 (with children 60 and 80). All BST properties hold.
rubric.acceptable: Describes a valid BST with the correct keys but one minor placement error (e.g., 35 placed as right child of 30 instead of left child of 40).
rubric.poor: Describes a tree that violates the BST property (e.g., 35 placed in the right subtree of 55) or omits multiple keys.

rubric.criterion: Correct tree after deleting 30 using in-order successor
rubric.excellent: Describes that 30's key is replaced by 35 (the in-order successor, smallest in the right subtree), and the original 35 node is removed (it had no children, so just deleted). Tree remains valid.
rubric.acceptable: Correctly replaces 30 with the successor but describes the successor deletion incorrectly (e.g., assumes successor had a child that was mishandled).
rubric.poor: Does not use the in-order successor method, or produces a tree that violates the BST property.

rubric.criterion: Explanation of why in-order successor preserves BST property
rubric.excellent: States that the successor is the smallest key larger than the deleted key, so placing it at the deleted node's position keeps all left-subtree keys smaller and all right-subtree keys larger. Also notes the successor has at most one child, so its deletion is simple.
rubric.acceptable: Gives a correct but vague explanation (e.g., 'it keeps the order') without mentioning the successor's minimal property or its single-child guarantee.
rubric.poor: Explanation is incorrect or missing entirely.

points: Search, insert and delete all cost O(h); balanced trees keep h = O(log n), sorted insertion makes h = n − 1.
The iterative search loop checks null before key comparison to avoid null reference errors.
Insert creates a new leaf where the search fell off the tree; duplicates are not inserted (distinct keys assumed).
Delete a leaf by setting the parent's child pointer to null.
Delete a node with one child by replacing the node with its child (update the parent's pointer).
Delete a node with two children by copying the in-order successor's key, then deleting the successor (which has at most one child).
In-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order.
